SLDR: Defending Against Malicious Fine-tuning via Selective Layers Recovery and Dynamic Routing

Hui Zhang ††thanks: These authors contributed equally. Affiliation: North China Electric Power University Affiliation: Southeast University Email: 220265641@seu.edu.cn    Yachao Yuan11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Soochow University Email: chao910904@suda.edu.cn    Jiayun Wang Affiliation: North China Electric Power University Email: 220262221153@ncepu.edu.cn    Yuanzhuo Li Affiliation: North China Electric Power University Email: 220252221023@ncepu.edu.cn    Hongtao Wang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: North China Electric Power University Affiliation: Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Computing for Complex Energy SystemsMinistry of Education Email: wanght@ncepu.edu.cn    Yali Yuan Affiliation: Southeast University Email: yaliyuan@seu.edu.cn
Abstract

Fine-tuning-as-a-service enables users to adapt aligned large language models (LLMs) to specialized tasks, but malicious fine-tuning can erode refusal behavior while preserving task performance on legitimate inputs. We revisit recent layer-wise safety diagnostics and find that safety sensitivity is signed: scaling different layers can strengthen refusal, weaken it, or have little effect. Motivated by this observation, we propose SLDR, a post-fine-tuning defense based on Selective Layers Recovery and Dynamic Routing. SLDR trains a LoRA recovery adapter only on the layers with the maximum and minimum sensitivity scores in the signed spectrum, and uses representation-based dynamic routing inference to activate the adapter only for malicious queries. Across four model architectures, five downstream tasks, and four harmful benchmarks, SLDR substantially reduces harmful outputs while preserving downstream utility. On Llama3.1/SST2, SLDR reduces the average harmful score from 11.54 to 0.08 while maintaining downstream accuracy, and the harmful score remains near zero under poisoning ratios up to 0.9. The code is available at https://github.com/Stardust457/SLDR.

This paper contains offensive and harmful examples.

1 Introduction

Fine-tuning-as-a-service enables users to adapt aligned LLMs with their own data, facilitating domain-specific customization. However, the same interface can be exploited by attackers to compromise the model’s safety alignment. By mixing a small number of harmful instruction-response pairs into otherwise benign task data, malicious fine-tuning can induce the model to respond to harmful queries while still retaining the intended task behavior on legitimate inputs Huang et al. (2024b); Lermen et al. (2023); Li et al. (2025d); Yi et al. (2024). This creates a recovery challenge for the service provider: how to restore refusal behavior without sacrificing the utility gained from user-provided data.

Existing defenses include alignment-phase defense, fine-tuning constraints, and post-compromise repair Hu et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2025a); Huang et al. (2024a); Huang et al. (2025b); Huang et al. (2024c); Peng et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026). Their limitations fall into two categories. The first constrains fine-tuning before harmful samples are learned, but may fail to generalize to unseen attacks. The second relies on coarse-grained model-level recovery after fine-tuning, such as perturbing weights or pruning harmful parameters, entangling safety repair with task-specific behavior, making it difficult to restore refusal capabilities without compromising benign task performance.

This motivates us to shift from coarse model-level recovery to layer-wise diagnosis. Prior work has shown that safety-relevant layers can be localized by perturbing layer parameters and observing changes in refusal behavior Li et al. (2025a); Li et al. (2025c). Yet these diagnostics mainly reveal where safety behavior is concentrated, not the direction of each layer’s effect. In other words, they do not distinguish whether a layer reinforces refusal or weakens it. We therefore turn layer-wise scaling into a signed diagnostic and ask: which layers make refusal more likely when strengthened, and which suppress it?

We instantiate this layer-wise diagnosis with a lightweight scaling probe. For each layer, we perturb its attention and feed-forward weights and measure the change in refusal on over-refusal prompts. As shown in Figure 1, the resulting sensitivity scores form a signed spectrum: some layers make refusal stronger when scaled, some make it weaker, and many have little effect. This suggests a recovery strategy that treats layers differently according to their effect on refusal. Motivated by this observation, we propose SLDR, a post-fine-tuning defense based on Selective Layers Recovery and Dynamic Routing. After task adaptation, SLDR trains a LoRA recovery adapter only on the layers with the maximum and minimum sensitivity scores in the signed spectrum. Layers with near-zero scores are largely insensitive to refusal under the probe, indicating that adjusting them would have minimal impact on refusal behavior. At inference time, malicious scores are computed by extracting representations. Harmful queries whose malicious scores exceed the threshold activate the adapter, while benign task queries falling below continue to use the unmodified fine-tuned model.

We evaluate SLDR under LoRA-based malicious fine-tuning across Llama3.1, Llama3 Grattafiori et al. (2024), Qwen2.5 Yang et al. (2024), and Mistral-v0.2 Jiang et al. (2023), covering five downstream tasks and four harmful benchmarks. In the default Llama3.1/SST2 setting, SLDR reduces the average harmful score from 11.54 to 0.08 while matching downstream accuracy, and it remains near zero under poisoning ratios up to 0.9. Our contributions are threefold.

  • •

    We move beyond locating safety-sensitive layers and identify a signed layer-wise pattern in refusal behavior: scaling different layers can increase, decrease, or have little effect on refusal.

  • •

    We propose SLDR, a post-fine-tuning defense that turns this signed diagnosis into selective recovery by training a LoRA recovery adapter only on the layers with the maximum/minimum sensitivity scores in the spectrum, and activating it conditionally at inference.

  • •

    We conduct extensive experiments across model architectures, downstream tasks, poisoning ratios, and harmful benchmarks, showing that SLDR substantially reduces harmful outputs while preserving the task behavior acquired during fine-tuning.

2 Related Work

Alignment-stage and fine-tuning-stage defenses. Existing defenses can be classified by the stage at which they intervene. Alignment-stage methods harden the model before user adaptation through perturbation-aware alignment Huang et al. (2025b); Huang et al. (2024c), data and representation hardening Liu et al. (2024); Rosati et al. (2024), tamper-resistant alignment Tamirisa et al. (2024), or defensive response guidance Chen et al. (2025b). Fine-tuning-stage methods control adaptation by filtering or scoring data Hu et al. (2025), regularizing updates Kim et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025b); Wu et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2026), alternating safety and task objectives Huang et al. (2024a), or shaping safety objectives and augmenting safety data Peng et al. (2025); Xiao et al. (2026). Latent adversarial training Casper et al. (2024) provides a related training-time robustness strategy. These methods typically require training-pipeline access and may additionally rely on safety data or scorers.

Post-fine-tuning-stage defenses. These methods repair a model after fine-tuning has compromised safety. Representative approaches include pruning Huang et al. (2025a), perturbation Wang et al. (2025), subspace or localized parameter recovery Hsu et al. (2024); Yi et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2025), rollback Yang et al. (2025), data-efficient realignment with One-shot FT Zhang et al. (2026), and inference-time intervention Jiang and Pan (2025), aiming to restore refusal behavior while limiting utility loss. SLDR also belongs to this post-fine-tuning setting, yet it differs by localizing recovery to a small set of safety-sensitive layers and applying the adapter conditionally rather than as a fixed model-level intervention.

Layer-wise safety analysis. Recent work demonstrates that refusal behavior is not uniformly distributed across layers. Safety Layers Li et al. (2025c) and LARF Li et al. (2025a) identify safety-relevant layers to protect during fine-tuning or use their representations to filter unsafe training examples. These studies motivate layer-local defenses, but their localization criteria do not explicitly distinguish whether a layer increases or decreases refusal. We extend this diagnostic by introducing a signed measure that separates layers that enhance refusal from those that suppress it, and leverage both ends of the spectrum for selective post-fine-tuning recovery. A more detailed related work is provided in Appendix E.

3 Signed Layer-wise Diagnosis and Analysis

To move beyond locating safety-relevant layers, we use layer-wise scaling as a signed diagnostic.

3.1 Sensitivity Score Calculation

Following prior work Li et al. (2025a); Li et al. (2025c), we perturb one layer at a time and measure how the model’s refusal behavior changes on an over-refusal dataset. The resulting score is used only to select recovery layers.

Module Weight Scaling. Let ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} be an aligned LLM with LL transformer layers. For layer l∈{0,…,L−1}l\in\{0,\dots,L-1\} and scaling factor α>0\alpha>0, we scale its attention and feed-forward network weights 𝐖(l)\mathbf{W}^{(l)} by (1±α)(1\pm\alpha) while keeping all other layers fixed via 𝐖(l)±=(1±α)​𝐖(l)\mathbf{W}^{(l)\pm}=(1\pm\alpha)\mathbf{W}^{(l)}. This produces an amplified variant ℳl,α+\mathcal{M}_{l,\alpha}^{+} and a suppressed variant ℳl,α−\mathcal{M}_{l,\alpha}^{-} for each layer. Scaling is applied to the aligned model before malicious fine-tuning, so the probe measures the layer’s role in the original refusal behavior.

Refusal Counting. We probe ℳl,α±\mathcal{M}_{l,\alpha}^{\pm} on an over-refusal dataset 𝒟reject\mathcal{D}_{\text{reject}}, which contains benign instructions with safety-related terms (e.g., “kill time”). Let ℳl,α±​(x)\mathcal{M}_{l,\alpha}^{\pm}(x) denote the response generated by the scaled model. The refusal count is

cl±​(α)=|{x∈𝒟reject∣IsRefusal​(ℳl,α±​(x))=True}|,c_{l}^{\pm}(\alpha)=\left|\left\{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{reject}}\mid\text{IsRefusal}\left(\mathcal{M}_{l,\alpha}^{\pm}(x)\right)=\text{True}\right\}\right|, (1)

where IsRefusal​(⋅)\text{IsRefusal}(\cdot) is detailed in Appendix A.1.

Sensitivity Score. We summarize each layer with a signed sensitivity score κl\kappa_{l}. Let Δl​(α)\Delta_{l}(\alpha) be the difference in refusal counts between amplified and suppressed scaling:

Δl​(α)=cl+​(α)−cl−​(α).\Delta_{l}(\alpha)=c_{l}^{+}(\alpha)-c_{l}^{-}(\alpha). (2)

We define κl\kappa_{l} as the maximum normalized signed change over a candidate set 𝒜\mathcal{A}:

κl=maxα∈𝒜⁡Δl​(α)α,\kappa_{l}=\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{\Delta_{l}(\alpha)}{\alpha}, (3)

where 𝒜={0.1,0.2}\mathcal{A}=\{0.1,0.2\} following Li et al. (2025a). A positive κl\kappa_{l} indicates that strengthening layer ll increases refusal, while a negative κl\kappa_{l} indicates that strengthening the layer suppresses refusal. Layers with scores near zero are largely insensitive to refusal under this probe.

3.2 Layer Sensitivity Analysis

Figure 1 shows the signed sensitivity scores for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, with additional model families reported in Appendix D.2. The first observation is that refusal sensitivity is highly non-uniform. Only a small subset of layers produces large changes in refusal, while many layers remain close to zero. This suggests that updating every layer during safety recovery is unnecessary: layers with near-zero scores provide little refusal-related signal under the probe and are unlikely to offer much marginal benefit.

The second observation is that sensitivity is directional. Positive layers increase refusal when strengthened, whereas negative layers decrease refusal when strengthened. The negative side is therefore not just “less safe” in a vague sense; it captures layers whose perturbation suppresses refusal under the same diagnostic. A recovery method that only targets positive safety layers may miss this complementary failure mode.

Together, these observations suggest that recovery should be selective and directional. Rather than updating the whole model, a defense should focus on layers that exert the strongest signed effects on refusal, while leaving near-neutral layers untouched to reduce unnecessary interference with task-specific behavior. The next section turns this diagnostic into a concrete post-fine-tuning recovery strategy.

4 Selective Layers Recovery and Dynamic Routing

SLDR consists of three components, as shown in Figure 2. First, it uses the signed diagnosis from Section 3 to select the two layers at the ends of the sensitivity spectrum, lminl_{\text{min}} and lmaxl_{\text{max}}. Second, after malicious fine-tuning, it trains a compact LoRA recovery adapter only on these two layers using a small alignment dataset 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}. Third, at inference time, a representation-based maliciousness score decides whether to activate the recovery adapter, so benign queries can use the task-adapted model directly.

4.1 Layer Selection

Given layer-wise sensitivity scores {κl}l=0L−1\{\kappa_{l}\}_{l=0}^{L-1}, SLDR selects the two endpoints of the signed spectrum:

lmin=arg⁡minl∈{0,…,L−1}​κl,lmax=arg⁡maxl∈{0,…,L−1}​κl.l_{\text{min}}=\underset{l\in\{0,\dots,L-1\}}{\arg\min}\,\kappa_{l},\quad l_{\text{max}}=\underset{l\in\{0,\dots,L-1\}}{\arg\max}\,\kappa_{l}. (4)

lmaxl_{\text{max}} has the strongest refusal-enhancing effect under the probe, while lminl_{\text{min}} has the strongest refusal-suppressing effect. We train recovery adapters on both endpoints: the positive endpoint reinforces refusal-supporting components, and the negative endpoint repairs components associated with refusal suppression. Layers with near-zero scores are left unchanged because they provide little refusal signal and may introduce unnecessary interference with task-specific behavior. Section 5.2 verifies the benefit of using both selected layers. We provide the algorithm for layer selection in Appendix C.1.

4.2 Two-stage Fine-tuning with Safety Recovery

Stage 1: Downstream Task Fine-Tuning. Let ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} be the original aligned LLM, and let 𝒟ft\mathcal{D}_{\text{ft}} denote the clean downstream task dataset. In malicious fine-tuning, the user does not submit 𝒟ft\mathcal{D}_{\text{ft}} directly. Instead, the submitted training set retains a benign subset of task examples and injects harmful instruction-response pairs:

𝒟train=𝒟ft′∪𝒟poison,\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{ft}}^{\prime}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}}, (5)

where 𝒟ft′⊆𝒟ft\mathcal{D}_{\text{ft}}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\text{ft}} provides the legitimate task-adaptation signal, and 𝒟poison\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}} teaches the model to comply with harmful requests. The poison ratio ρ=|𝒟poison|/|𝒟train|\rho=|\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}}|/|\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}| controls the attack strength. The service provider treats 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} as the user-provided fine-tuning data and applies LoRA fine-tuning Hu et al. (2022):

minΔ​θtask⁡𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟train​[−log⁡pθ0+Δ​θtask​(y∣x)].\min_{\Delta\theta_{\text{task}}}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}\left[-\log p_{\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{\text{task}}}(y\mid x)\right]. (6)

This yields an attacked model ℳatt\mathcal{M}_{\text{att}} that preserves task performance but has weakened refusal behavior.

Stage 2: Safety Recovery. Starting from ℳatt\mathcal{M}_{\text{att}}, SLDR trains LoRA updates only on lminl_{\text{min}} and lmaxl_{\text{max}}, freezing all other parameters. Given an alignment dataset 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}} of harmful prompts paired with safe responses, the recovery update is learned by

minΔ​θrecovery⁡𝔼(xharm,ysafe)∼𝒟safe​[−log⁡pθatt+Δ​θrecovery​(ysafe∣xharm)].\min_{\Delta\theta_{\text{recovery}}}\mathbb{E}_{(x_{\text{harm}},y_{\text{safe}})\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}}\left[-\log p_{\theta_{\text{att}}+\Delta\theta_{\text{recovery}}}(y_{\text{safe}}\mid x_{\text{harm}})\right]. (7)

The resulting model ℳrec\mathcal{M}_{\text{rec}} restores refusal behavior through a layer-local adapter, reducing the chance that safety recovery overwrites task-specific knowledge acquired in Stage 1.

4.3 Representation-based Dynamic Routing Inference

Activating the recovery adapter for every query can unnecessarily affect benign task inputs. SLDR therefore routes queries according to a representation-based maliciousness score. We provide the algorithm for the representation-based dynamic routing inference in Appendix C.2.

Reference Representation Construction. We use two small reference sets as anchors for routing, i.e., harmful reference prompts and benign reference prompts. Formally, let 𝒟harmful={xiharmful}i=1N\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}}=\{x^{\text{harmful}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and 𝒟benign={xibenign}i=1N\mathcal{D}_{\text{benign}}=\{x^{\text{benign}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} denote these two sets. For a prompt x∈𝒟harmful∪𝒟benignx\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{benign}}, let hlmax​(x)h_{l_{\text{max}}}(x) denote the last-token hidden state output by layer lmaxl_{\text{max}} of ℳrec\mathcal{M}_{\text{rec}}. We normalize it as follows:

r⁡(x)=hlmax​(x)‖hlmax​(x)‖2.r(x)=\frac{h_{l_{\text{max}}}(x)}{\|h_{l_{\text{max}}}(x)\|_{2}}. (8)

This gives harmful and benign reference sets ℛu={r⁡(xiharmful)}i=1N\mathcal{R}_{u}=\{r(x_{i}^{\text{harmful}})\}_{i=1}^{N} and ℛs={r⁡(xibenign)}i=1N\mathcal{R}_{s}=\{r(x_{i}^{\text{benign}})\}_{i=1}^{N}.

Malicious Score Computation. For a test example (xtest,ytest)∈𝒟test(x^{\text{test}},y^{\text{test}})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}, we compute the representation r⁡(xtest)r(x^{\text{test}}) of the prompt xtestx^{\text{test}} and compare its cosine similarities to the harmful and benign reference sets:

δi(xtest)=cos(r(xtest),r(xiharmful))−cos(r(xtest),r(xibenign)),i=1,…,N.\delta_{i}(x^{\text{test}})=\cos\!\left(r(x^{\text{test}}),\,r(x_{i}^{\text{harmful}})\right)-\cos\!\left(r(x^{\text{test}}),\,r(x_{i}^{\text{benign}})\right),\quad i=1,\ldots,N. (9)

The malicious score is the mean similarity gap:

Smalicious​(xtest)=1N​∑i=1Nδi​(xtest).S_{\text{malicious}}(x^{\text{test}})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{i}(x^{\text{test}}). (10)

Dynamic Routing. If Smalicious​(xtest)>τS_{\text{malicious}}(x^{\text{test}})>\tau, SLDR routes xtestx^{\text{test}} through the recovered model; otherwise, it uses the attacked task-adapted model without the recovery adapter:

y^​(xtest)={ℳrec​(xtest),if ​Smalicious​(xtest)>τ,ℳatt​(xtest),otherwise,\hat{y}(x^{\text{test}})=\begin{cases}\mathcal{M}_{\text{rec}}(x^{\text{test}}),&\text{if }S_{\text{malicious}}(x^{\text{test}})>\tau,\\ \mathcal{M}_{\text{att}}(x^{\text{test}}),&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (11)

where y^​(xtest)\hat{y}(x^{\text{test}}) denotes the model-generated response. We use τ=0\tau=0 by default and study its effect in Section 5.2.

5 Experiments

Datasets and Models. For a fair comparison, we follow the experimental setup of Hu et al. (2025). The alignment dataset 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}} is drawn from the dataset of Hu et al. (2025) (an extended version of BeaverTails Ji et al. (2023)); the poison dataset 𝒟poison\mathcal{D}_{\text{poison}} is sampled from Ji et al. (2023). The two sets are non-overlapping. Downstream tasks include SST2 Socher et al. (2013), AGNEWS Zhang et al. (2015), GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021), AlpacaEval Li et al. (2023), and Magicoder Wei et al. (2023). Safety evaluation is conducted on the BeaverTails test set, DirectHarm4 Lyu et al. (2024), HarmBench Mazeika et al. (2024), and HEx-PHI Qi et al. (2023). The reference datasets 𝒟harmful\mathcal{D}_{\text{harmful}} and 𝒟benign\mathcal{D}_{\text{benign}} are sourced from Li et al. (2025a) and Zhang et al. (2025), respectively. Detailed descriptions of downstream datasets are provided in Appendix A.2. We evaluate on the following models: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct (Llama3.1) Grattafiori et al. (2024), Llama3-8B-Instruct (Llama3) Grattafiori et al. (2024), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen2.5) Yang et al. (2024), and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 (Mistral-v0.2) Jiang et al. (2023). To simulate harmful fine-tuning, 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} is constructed by mixing a fraction ρ\rho of poison samples with a fraction 1−ρ1-\rho of downstream task data, with a total size of |𝒟train|\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert. The default setting is ρ=0.1\rho=0.1 and |𝒟train|=1000\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert=1000 (|𝒟train|=700\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert=700 for AlpacaEval).

Baselines. We compare our method against state-of-the-art baselines: Antidote Huang et al. (2025a), Panacea Wang et al. (2025), One-shot FT Zhang et al. (2026), Lisa Huang et al. (2024a), STAR-DSS Peng et al. (2025), and BDS Hu et al. (2025), along with SFT Hu et al. (2022) (supervised fine-tuning, no defense applied) as the worst-case reference. Baseline details are in Appendix A.3.

Metrics. Following Hu et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025), we adopt two evaluation metrics:

  • •

    Harmful Score (HS): We use Llama-Guard-3-8B Grattafiori et al. (2024) to classify model outputs as safe/unsafe. The harmful score is defined as the percentage of unsafe outputs over all outputs.

  • •

    Finetune Accuracy (FA): The model’s accuracy on the corresponding downstream task test set.

Further evaluation details are provided in Appendix A.4.

Implementation Details. We apply LoRA Hu et al. (2022) for efficient fine-tuning. For downstream fine-tuning, we use AdamW Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) (lr=1×10−5\text{lr}=1\times 10^{-5}, weight decay=0.1\text{weight decay}=0.1, batch size=10\text{batch size}=10), training for 20 epochs (100 for AlpacaEval). The safety recovery stage shares the same batch size and epoch count with lr=5×10−4\text{lr}=5\times 10^{-4}. The threshold τ\tau is set to 0, and the size of 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}} is |𝒟safe|=100\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}\rvert=100. For a more detailed introduction, see Appendix A.5.

5.1 Main Results

Comparison with SOTA Baselines. Table 1 presents a systematic comparison across harmful ratios ρ∈{0,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2}\rho\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2\} on Llama3.1/SST2 with |𝒟train|=1000\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert=1000. SLDR achieves an average HS of 0.08 and an average FA of 92.32, simultaneously outperforming most baselines on both metrics. Prior defenses face an inherent safety-utility tension: Lisa and Antidote reduce average HS to 1.70 and 1.50, but their average FA drops to 74.17 and 84.86, losses of 18.2 and 7.5 points relative to SFT (92.39). Panacea and One-shot FT preserve utility better (average FA of 89.29 and 90.55), but their defense weakens as ρ\rho increases, with Panacea’s HS rising from 1.20 at ρ=0\rho=0 to 7.80 at ρ=0.2\rho=0.2. BDS offers the strongest prior defense (average HS of 1.68, FA of 91.79), yet SLDR reduces HS by another order of magnitude without any utility cost. Even at ρ=0.2\rho=0.2, SLDR holds HS at 0.20 while SFT reaches 20.90. This advantage stems from the targeted recovery of lminl_{\text{min}} and lmaxl_{\text{max}} and the representation-based dynamic routing that activates the safety LoRA only when malicious intent is detected, thereby mitigating downstream task loss and providing a more robust and efficient defense for fine-tuning as a service.

Robustness Across Different Downstream Tasks. Moving from the primary benchmark, Table 3 evaluates SLDR across four tasks of varying format and complexity (SST2, AGNEWS, GSM8K, and AlpacaEval) under default settings. SLDR consistently achieves near-zero HS (≤0.20\leq 0.20) across all tasks while maintaining utility levels virtually identical to undefended SFT. On GSM8K, SLDR preserves exactly the same FA as SFT (72.10) while reducing HS from 12.30 to 0.00. On AGNEWS, SLDR similarly matches SFT’s FA (83.00) with HS of only 0.10. This stands in sharp contrast to Lisa and Antidote, which suffer FA drops of up to 12.6 points on AGNEWS (70.40 and 71.50 vs. SFT’s 83.00), suggesting that their coarse model-level constraints disrupt the structured reasoning capabilities acquired during fine-tuning. The consistent performance across tasks of varying format and complexity validates that selective layer recovery and dynamic routing effectively decouple task-specific learning from safety restoration, ensuring robust protection regardless of task type.

Robustness Across Different Model Architectures. To assess whether SLDR’s signed sensitivity signal generalizes beyond a single model family, Table 3 extends the evaluation to Llama3.1, Llama3, Qwen2.5, and Mistral-v0.2 under default settings on SST2. The magnitude of safety degradation under SFT varies substantially across architectures: Mistral-v0.2 is exceptionally vulnerable (HS = 49.40), while Qwen2.5 is considerably more resilient (HS = 3.20), reflecting differences in pretraining and alignment procedures. The signed sensitivity spectrum is architecture-agnostic: SLDR’s diagnostic reliably identifies lminl_{\text{min}} and lmaxl_{\text{max}} across all four model families, yielding HS ≤0.20\leq 0.20 in every case. On Mistral-v0.2, where existing baselines struggle significantly (Panacea achieves HS of 37.90, Lisa 12.80, and STAR-DSS a lower HS of 7.40, but with FA collapsing to 60.78), SLDR reduces HS to 0.10 without sacrificing utility (FA = 95.07, nearly matching SFT’s 95.18). FA is mostly preserved across all architectures, confirming that the LoRA recovery adapter does not interfere with task-specific knowledge. These results demonstrate that the directional layer-wise signal exploited by SLDR is a general property of aligned LLMs rather than an artifact of any particular model family.

Robustness Across Different LLM Judge. To verify that our results are not artifacts of the Llama-Guard-3-8B Grattafiori et al. (2024), Table 4 re-evaluates SLDR and the two baselines (BDS and One-shot FT) using GPT-4o as an independent judge across ρ∈{0,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2}\rho\in\{0,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2\} with |𝒟train|=1000\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert=1000. GPT-4o provides a 5-point scale rating, where HS=1\text{HS}=1 represents the safest situation and HS=5\text{HS}=5 represents the most unsafe situation. SLDR consistently achieves the lowest harmful scores (average 1.09), outperforming BDS (1.47) and One-shot FT (1.81) across all poisoning ratios. Notably, the relative ordering of HS across different methods remains consistent under both judges, confirming that SLDR’s safety advantage does not stem from a specific LLM judge.

Robustness Across Different Poisoning Ratios. Having established SLDR’s advantage under moderate attack strengths, Table 5 stress-tests representative methods at extreme poisoning ratios ρ∈{0.3,…,1.0}\rho\in\{0.3,\ldots,1.0\} with |𝒟train|=1000\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert=1000 on Llama3.1/SST2. Under standard fine-tuning (SFT), HS escalates rapidly with ρ\rho, reaching 36.70 at ρ=1.0\rho=1.0. BDS provides meaningful defense but exhibits a gradual upward drift (HS = 2.90 at ρ=0.3\rho=0.3, rising to 3.60 at ρ=1.0\rho=1.0), while One-shot FT deteriorates more sharply (HS = 5.00 to 8.00 over the same range). SLDR, by contrast, maintains near-zero toxicity throughout (HS ≤0.40\leq 0.40) with no discernible upward trend, even at ρ=0.9\rho=0.9 where poison samples outnumber clean samples by a ratio of 9:1, and at ρ=1.0\rho=1.0 where all training samples are harmful. We attribute this robustness to the layer-local nature of the recovery: since the LoRA adapter is confined to lminl_{\text{min}} and lmaxl_{\text{max}}, its recovery target remains well-defined. At the same time, FA is mostly preserved across all ratios, with SLDR’s FA matching or closely tracking SFT’s at every point.

Robustness Across Different Harmful Benchmarks. To test generalization beyond the BeaverTails, Table 7 evaluates SLDR on three additional benchmarks (DirectHarm4 Lyu et al. (2024), HarmBench Mazeika et al. (2024), and HEx-PHI Qi et al. (2023)) under default settings. SLDR achieves HS ≤1.75\leq 1.75 across all three, substantially outperforming BDS (10.25, 11.00, and 8.28) and One-shot FT (22.50, 17.50, and 15.52), the latter performing even worse than SFT. The consistent advantage across diverse harmful content categories suggests that the SLDR generalizes well to out-of-distribution harmful queries.

Robustness on a More Complex Task. Table 7 evaluates SLDR on Magicoder Wei et al. (2023), a challenging code generation task evaluated via HumanEval Chen et al. (2021). Code generation is a particularly demanding test case, as it requires precise syntactic and semantic reasoning. SLDR achieves HS = 0.10 while matching SFT’s FA (59.76). One-shot FT reduces neither HS nor FA to competitive levels (4.60 and 59.15, respectively). These results confirm that SLDR’s layer-local recovery does not interfere with complex generation capabilities, extending its applicability to specialized high-utility domains.

Robustness Across Different Sizes of |𝒟train|\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert. Table 9 examines whether SLDR scales as the training set grows from 500 to 2000 samples at ρ=0.1\rho=0.1. SFT’s HS escalates sharply with |𝒟train|\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert, from 3.50 at 500 samples to 30.70 at 2000, confirming that larger fine-tuning budgets amplify the attack even at a fixed poison ratio. BDS and One-shot FT maintain moderate defense (HS ≤4.10\leq 4.10) but incur non-trivial FA penalties relative to SFT. SLDR maintains HS ≤0.40\leq 0.40 across all sizes while exactly matching SFT’s FA at every point (e.g., 93.23 vs. 93.23 at |𝒟train|=2000\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert=2000). This scaling behavior demonstrates that SLDR’s performance is independent of the fine-tuning dataset size, maintaining low HS even under a large |𝒟train|\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert without any drop in FA.

Robustness Across Jailbreak Attacks. Table 9 evaluates SLDR against Zulu Yong et al. (2023), an encoding-based low-resource language attack, and IJP Shen et al. (2024), a hand-crafted prompt attack derived from real-world social media, on Llama3.1/SST2 under default settings. All methods show substantially elevated HS under the Zulu attack, reflecting the inadequacy of existing defense methods against low-resource language attacks. SLDR achieves the lowest HS on both attacks (61.53 under Zulu, 15.53 under IJP), demonstrating meaningful residual protection even against obfuscated inputs outside the distribution of 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}. Strengthening the routing mechanism against such distributional shifts remains a promising direction for future work. See Appendix A.6 for more details on the two jailbreak attacks.

Case Study. We evaluate the responses of our method and other baselines to malicious queries under default settings; see Appendix D.9 for details.

5.2 Ablation Study.

Impact of |𝒟safe|\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}\rvert. As shown in Figure 4, we investigate the effect of alignment dataset size |𝒟safe|\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}\rvert on SLDR under default settings on Llama3.1. With only |𝒟safe|=30\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}\rvert=30, the Harmful Score (HS) drops sharply to 0.3 and 0.2 on SST2 and AGNEWS, respectively, while Finetune Accuracy (FA) remains high. At |𝒟safe|=100\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}\rvert=100, HS reaches its minimum (0.0 and 0.1), with FA at 92.43 and 83.00. Further increasing |𝒟safe|\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}\rvert to 300 or 500 yields no additional safety benefit while incurring a marginal FA decline. These results demonstrate that our method requires only a small alignment dataset to restore LLM safety without compromising downstream task performance.

Impact of τ\tau. As illustrated in Figure 4, we evaluate the effect of threshold τ\tau on HS and FA using Llama3.1 on SST2 under default settings. Increasing τ\tau causes some harmful inputs to bypass the LoRA recovery adapter, raising HS; decreasing τ\tau forces benign inputs through the LoRA recovery adapter, degrading FA. Therefore, we adopt τ=0\tau=0 as our default, which maximally improves LLM safety without compromising downstream task performance.

Ablation on Layer Selection Choices. As shown in Table 11, selecting both lminl_{\text{min}} and lmaxl_{\text{max}} for recovery is essential, and the choice is motivated by the signed sensitivity spectrum. We use default settings and conduct experiments on the SST2 dataset. lmaxl_{\text{max}} carries the strongest refusal-enhancing signal and directly reinforces the model’s tendency to refuse harmful queries, while lminl_{\text{min}} is the layer most prone to corruption under malicious fine-tuning, whose recovery repairs the primary failure mode introduced by the attack. Using either endpoint alone addresses only half of this picture: on Qwen2.5, only lminl_{\text{min}} leaves HS at 0.80, and only lmaxl_{\text{max}} reduces HS to 0.20 but incurs a marginal FA cost. Targeting other layers entirely yields the worst HS (0.90 on Qwen2.5) with no FA benefit, confirming that near-zero sensitivity layers contribute little refusal-related signal and introduce unnecessary interference with task-specific behavior. The lmin+lmaxl_{\text{min}}+l_{\text{max}} combination attains the best overall profile on Mistral-v0.2 (HS=0.10, FA=95.07), demonstrating that the effectiveness of SLDR derives from targeting both ends of the signed sensitivity spectrum rather than from the number of layers updated.

Ablation on Representation-based Dynamic Routing Inference. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed Representation-based Dynamic Routing Inference (RDRI), we compare settings without and with RDRI on Llama3.1 across SST2 and AGNEWS (ρ=0.1\rho=0.1, |𝒟train|=1500\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\rvert=1500), as shown in Table 11. Removing RDRI yields only a marginal HS reduction but causes a dramatic FA drop, as the LoRA recovery adapter is uniformly applied to all queries, impairing performance on benign inputs.

5.3 Analysis

Comparison with Existing Layer-wise Statistics. To better understand the signed sensitivity identified by SLDR, we compare it with three existing layer-wise statistics on the same Llama3.1-8B-Instruct architecture (32 transformer layers, indexed 0–31): Panacea, Targeted Vaccine Liu et al. (2025), and Surgery Liu et al. (2026). Specifically, Panacea measures the magnitude of the optimized adaptive parameter perturbation, Targeted Vaccine measures the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm of harmful-data gradients on hidden embeddings, Surgery aggregates attention-head sink divergences within each layer, while SLDR measures the normalized signed change in refusal counts under layer amplification and suppression.

For Panacea, Targeted Vaccine, and Surgery, layers are ranked by their raw scores in descending order according to their respective criteria. For SLDR, we rank by |κl||\kappa_{l}| only for comparison, while the actual recovery explicitly selects the maximum and minimum endpoints of the signed spectrum.

As shown in Tables 12 and 13, these statistics identify partially overlapping but clearly non-identical safety-relevant layers. Panacea mainly emphasizes middle layers, Targeted Vaccine favors layer 0 and several layers around 16–19, and Surgery concentrates its Top-5 on layers 0–4. In contrast, SLDR’s Top-5 layers lie in the middle region (8–15).

More importantly, SLDR explicitly uses the sign of κl\kappa_{l} to distinguish opposite layer-level effects on refusal: κl>0\kappa_{l}>0 indicates that amplification increases refusal, whereas κl<0\kappa_{l}<0 indicates that amplification decreases refusal. For example, adjacent layers 12 and 13 have two of the largest |κl||\kappa_{l}| values but opposite effects (−185-185 versus +200+200). This directional information distinguishes SLDR from existing layer-wise statistics and motivates recovering both endpoints of the signed sensitivity spectrum.

6 Conclusion

We present SLDR, a post-fine-tuning defense against malicious fine-tuning of LLMs. By introducing a signed layer-wise sensitivity diagnostic, we identify that refusal behavior is governed by layers with directionally distinct effects. SLDR selectively trains a LoRA recovery adapter on the two most influential layers and employs representation-based dynamic routing to activate it only for harmful queries. Extensive experiments across multiple LLM architectures, downstream tasks, and harmful benchmarks demonstrate that SLDR effectively eliminates harmful outputs while fully preserving downstream task utility.

Contents

Appendix A More Details

A.1 Details of the Keyword-based Classifier

Following [23], the IsRefusal​(⋅)\text{IsRefusal}(\cdot) classifier is a lightweight keyword-based method used to determine whether a model output constitutes a refusal response. Given an LLM-generated string, the classifier first normalizes the text to lowercase and then checks for the presence of any predefined refusal keywords. If at least one keyword is matched, the response is classified as a refusal.

The keyword list and matching rule employed by the classifier are summarized below:

Formally, let ss denote the model output string and K={k1,k2,…,kn}K=\{k_{1},k_{2},\ldots,k_{n}\} the set of refusal keywords listed above. The classifier returns True if ∃ki∈K\exists\,k_{i}\in K such that kik_{i} is a substring of lowercase​(s)\texttt{lowercase}(s), and False otherwise. Here, lowercase​(⋅)\text{lowercase}(\cdot) is a function that converts all characters in a string to lowercase.

A.2 Details of Downstream Datasets

SST2 Dataset: SST2 [39] is a widely used English dataset for sentiment classification tasks. The dataset contains 11,855 individual sentences extracted from movie reviews, which are further parsed into 215,154 distinct phrases. Each phrase is assigned a sentiment label by three human annotators independently. In the SST2 dataset, the labels are simplified to a binary classification, namely positive (1) and negative (0), with neutral phrases excluded.

AGNEWS Dataset: AGNEWS [54] is a widely adopted benchmark in the field of text classification, comprising approximately 120,000 news articles evenly distributed across four topical categories: World, Sports, Business, and Science/Technology, with each category containing roughly 30,000 samples. This balanced label distribution makes it a reliable dataset for both training and evaluating classification models.

GSM8K Dataset: GSM8K [6] is a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in LLMs, comprising 8,500 high-quality grade school math word problems created by human writers, split into 7,500 training and 1,000 test samples. Each problem requires 2 to 8 reasoning steps using elementary arithmetic operations and is paired with a natural language solution. The dataset emphasizes high linguistic diversity and moderate difficulty, avoiding templated problems and concepts beyond early algebra.

AlpacaEval Dataset: AlpacaEval [25] is an instruction-following benchmark developed by the Tatsu Laboratory at Stanford University, containing 805 diverse instructions across a broad range of general-purpose user queries. In our experiments, 700 examples are used for downstream fine-tuning, while 104 non-overlapping examples are used for evaluation to measure the model’s generalization to unseen instructions.

Magicoder Dataset: Magicoder [42] is a synthetic code generation instruction-tuning dataset containing 75,000 programming problem-solution pairs generated by GPT-3.5-turbo-1106. The dataset is constructed by using randomly sampled code snippets from the open-source starcoderdata corpus as seed inputs to prompt a teacher model, producing diverse and realistic programming tasks that cover algorithm challenges, data science problems, library-based code completion, and full application development across multiple programming languages.

A.3 Details of Baselines

SFT: SFT fine-tunes the model via LoRA on user-uploaded datasets to achieve strong performance on specific downstream tasks. No defense mechanisms are applied during fine-tuning, representing the worst-case scenario following a malicious fine-tuning attack.

Antidote: Antidote [11] proposes a post-fine-tuning defense against harmful fine-tuning attacks. It identifies and prunes harmful model parameters using Wanda importance scores computed over a re-alignment dataset, remaining agnostic to fine-tuning hyperparameters. Experiments show it effectively reduces harmful scores with minimal downstream accuracy loss.

Panacea: Panacea [41] is a post-fine-tuning defense against harmful fine-tuning attacks. During fine-tuning, it jointly optimizes an adaptive perturbation via a max-max objective: the inner optimization finds the perturbation that maximally increases harmful loss (via gradient ascent), while the outer optimization minimizes fine-tuning loss. The perturbation is then added to the model weights after fine-tuning completes.

One-shot FT: One-shot FT [52] selects a single optimal safety example from a candidate set via bi-level optimization, then fine-tunes the compromised model with this one instance. Grounded in the low-rank structure of safety gradients, it fully restores alignment within minutes while preserving downstream task utility.

Lisa: Lisa [12] introduces a proximal term into a Bi-State Optimization framework during the user fine-tuning stage. It alternately optimizes over alignment and fine-tuning datasets, constraining parameter drift between state switches. This prevents harmful fine-tuning from erasing safety alignment while preserving downstream task performance.

STAR-DSS: STAR-DSS [33] introduces STAR (Safety Trajectory Assessment of Response), a token-level safety signal computed by querying a guardrail model on partial responses. During fine-tuning, DSS dynamically interpolates between cross-entropy and KL-divergence losses based on STAR scores, reinforcing safe content while suppressing unsafe segments without requiring external safe data.

BDS: BDS [10] formulates harmful fine-tuning defense as a Bayesian inference problem, learning a posterior distribution over per-sample safety weights conditioned on the fine-tuning and alignment datasets. Using Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics, it jointly updates model parameters and data weights with a softmax transformation, adaptively down-weighting harmful samples without requiring attack simulation.

A.4 Details of Evaluation

Following [10], for SST2, AGNEWS, GSM8K, and AlpacaEval, we sample 872, 1,000, 1,000, and 104 instances from their respective test sets for evaluation. For Magicoder, we evaluate using HumanEval [4] with 164 test samples.

Specifically, accuracy on SST2, AGNEWS, and GSM8K is computed by directly comparing model outputs against the ground-truth labels in the test set. For HumanEval, we report the pass@1 metric. Since AlpacaEval involves open-ended question answering, it is not amenable to straightforward quantitative measurement of FA. Following [10, 41], we employ the GPT-4o API to score the quality of model outputs, using the evaluation template below:

The scoring rubric assigns integer scores from 1 to 10, where 1 denotes the lowest output quality and 10 denotes the highest. The final score is obtained by averaging the scores across all test samples and multiplying by 10 to convert to a percentile scale.

A.5 Implementation Details

For parameter-efficient fine-tuning, we apply LoRA [9] to the query, key, and value projection matrices with LoRA rank r=32r=32 and LoRA α=4\alpha=4. All experiments use the AdamW [29] optimizer with a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, weight decay of 0.1, and batch size of 10. Following [10], we train for 20 epochs on SST2, AGNEWS, GSM8K, and Magicoder, and for 100 epochs on AlpacaEval to account for its larger task diversity. The safety recovery stage retains the same batch size and matches the number of training epochs used in the corresponding downstream fine-tuning run, while adopting a higher learning rate of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} to facilitate rapid safety realignment. The threshold τ\tau is set to 0, and the size of 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}} is |𝒟safe|=100\lvert\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}\rvert=100. All our experiments were conducted on a single A100-PCIE-40GB GPU.

A.6 Details of Jailbreak Attacks

Zulu: Zulu [51] is an encoding-based jailbreak attack. It leverages the inherent vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) in low-resource languages (such as Zulu) by translating malicious inputs into these languages. By exploiting the diminished safety alignment of models in such linguistic contexts, Zulu effectively bypasses internal security detection mechanisms.

IJP: IJP [38] represents a category of hand-crafted jailbreak attacks. These attacks are meticulously engineered by human adversaries based on a profound understanding of LLMs’ underlying mechanisms and vulnerabilities to circumvent safety alignment. The constituent prompts are derived from real-world jailbreak samples observed in production environments and shared by users across social media platforms.

Appendix B Threat Model and Assumptions

B.1 Threat Model

The fine-tuning-as-a-service paradigm allows users to fine-tune LLMs hosted by service providers via APIs, but introduces potential security and regulatory risks [13, 36]. Attackers operate in a black-box manner, submitting only fine-tuning data through open API interfaces without access to model weights or gradients. Their goal is to craft malicious fine-tuning data that bypasses the model’s safety alignment while preserving downstream task performance. Service providers, as defenders, retain full access to the model’s architecture and weights.

B.2 Assumptions

We assume that the service provider maintains an alignment dataset 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}, which contains harmful prompt-safe response pairs used to restore the safety alignment of LLMs. The availability of such alignment datasets has been discussed in prior works [10, 11, 15].

Appendix D More Experiments

D.1 Results of Refusal Counting

Figures 5, 6, 7, and 8 illustrate the layer-wise refusal count results for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 under scaling factors α∈{0.1,0.2}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.2\}. A consistent trend emerges across all four LLMs: for specific layers, amplifying weights leads to a decrease in refusal counts while scaling them down results in an increase, suggesting that these layers attenuate the model’s refusal capability. Conversely, for other layers, weight amplification increases refusal counts while scaling down decreases them, indicating that these layers enhance refusal behavior. Additionally, certain layers exhibit negligible changes in refusal counts regardless of scaling, implying they are largely irrelevant to the model’s refusal response. Given this ubiquitous phenomenon across diverse architectures, performing layer-wise diagnosis and quantifying each layer’s contribution through specific metrics can better inform the research and development of defense mechanisms.

D.2 Results of Layer-wise Sensitivity Scores

Figures 9, 10 and 11 illustrate the results of our Signed Layer-wise Diagnosis (SLD) on Llama3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, revealing the heterogeneous sensitivity of various layers toward safety refusal behavior. Specifically, positive sensitivity scores (green) indicate layers that enhance the model’s refusal response upon weight scaling, while negative scores (red) pinpoint layers that undermine it. The observed variance across the layer spectrum provides the empirical justification for our Selective Layers Recovery strategy. By targeting only the extreme layers in the sensitivity spectrum (i.e., lminl_{\text{min}} and lmaxl_{\text{max}}) for restoration, the SLDR framework effectively mitigates safety degradation with minimal parameter updates, thereby preserving the model’s utility on downstream tasks.

D.3 Multi-seed Stability Analysis

To examine whether the performance of SLDR is sensitive to the choice of random seed, we repeat the experiments under four random seeds, {0,1,2,42}\{0,1,2,42\}. We use Llama3.1 with the SST2 dataset under the default setting of ρ=0.1\rho=0.1 and |𝒟train|=1000|\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}|=1000, and compare SLDR with BDS and One-shot FT. For each method, we report the Harmful Score (HS) and Finetune Accuracy (FA) under each seed, together with the mean and standard deviation across the four runs.

As shown in Table 14, SLDR exhibits stable performance across all four random seeds. Its HS remains between 0.00 and 0.20, resulting in an average HS of 0.08±0.100.08\pm 0.10, while maintaining an average FA of 92.92±0.3392.92\pm 0.33. In comparison, BDS and One-shot FT achieve average HS values of 1.88±0.361.88\pm 0.36 and 4.18±0.324.18\pm 0.32, respectively, with lower average FA. These results demonstrate that the safety and utility performance of SLDR is consistent across different random seeds and that the observed performance gains are not specific to a particular seed.

D.4 Transfer to Full-parameter Fine-tuning

To evaluate whether SLDR remains effective under a different downstream fine-tuning method, we conduct full-parameter fine-tuning experiments on Llama3.1 with the SST2 dataset under the default setting of ρ=0.1\rho=0.1 and |𝒟train|=1000|\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}|=1000. We compare SLDR with BDS and One-shot FT, while the safety recovery stage of SLDR still uses the LoRA recovery adapter.

As shown in Table 15, the Harmful Scores of BDS and One-shot FT increase substantially under full-parameter downstream fine-tuning, reaching 47.70 and 51.10, respectively. In contrast, SLDR maintains a Harmful Score of only 1.10 while preserving a Finetune Accuracy of 92.55. These results demonstrate that SLDR remains effective when malicious downstream fine-tuning is performed with full-parameter updates, indicating that its defense is not limited to LoRA-based downstream fine-tuning.

D.5 Computational Overhead

We further evaluate the computational overhead introduced by SLDR on Llama3.1. We measure both the one-time cost of layer-wise probing and the online inference overhead introduced by representation-based dynamic routing. For inference-time evaluation, we use 1,000 prompts from BeaverTails with a fixed generation length of 64 tokens.

As shown in Table 16, probing all 32 layers requires only 0.3663 hours and is performed once offline for layer selection. At inference time, standard SFT requires 0.3121 seconds per prompt, whereas SLDR requires 0.3293 seconds per prompt, corresponding to an additional overhead of only 0.0172 seconds per prompt. The SLDR inference time includes representation extraction, malicious score computation, dynamic routing, and response generation. Therefore, the layer-selection procedure introduces only a one-time offline cost, while the representation-based dynamic routing mechanism incurs a modest online inference overhead.

D.6 Additional Comparisons

To further evaluate SLDR, we compare it against the original aligned Llama3.1 model before downstream fine-tuning and EnchTable [44]. For EnchTable, we use our paper’s default Llama3.1/SST2 fine-tuning configuration with ρ=0.1\rho=0.1 and |𝒟train|=1000|\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}|=1000. All methods are evaluated using the same test sets and generation settings.

We first report the Harmful Score (HS) under the Zulu and IJP jailbreak attacks. As shown in Table 17, SLDR achieves an HS of 61.53 on Zulu, which is 5.29 percentage points lower than the original aligned model (66.82) and 11.18 points lower than EnchTable (72.71). On IJP, SLDR obtains an HS of 15.53, compared with 12.94 for the original aligned model and 13.53 for EnchTable. These results show that SLDR provides stronger protection under the Zulu attack, while a small gap remains under IJP, highlighting the challenge posed by jailbreak-induced distribution shifts.

We additionally report HS on BeaverTails, which is used for harmfulness evaluation in our main experiments, together with SST2 Finetune Accuracy (FA). As shown in Table 18, SLDR achieves an HS of 0.00 on BeaverTails, compared with 1.50 for both the original aligned model and EnchTable. Notably, the HS of SLDR is even lower than that of the original aligned model, indicating that the safety recovery stage can further strengthen the model’s refusal behavior. Meanwhile, SLDR achieves an SST2 FA of 92.43, matching undefended SFT and exceeding EnchTable by 3.78 percentage points. The original aligned model has not been fine-tuned on SST2, and therefore its lower FA of 70.64 is expected.

D.7 Impact of Recovery Epochs

To evaluate the sensitivity of SLDR to the number of recovery epochs, we vary the training epochs of the safety recovery stage on Llama3.1 with the SST2 dataset under the default setting of ρ=0.1\rho=0.1 and |𝒟train|=1000|\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}|=1000. We evaluate recovery epochs in {5,10,20,30,40,50}\{5,10,20,30,40,50\}, where 20 epochs is the default setting.

As shown in Table 19, the safety recovery stage converges within 10 epochs, while the default setting of 20 epochs achieves the best observed performance. Further increasing the number of recovery epochs brings no additional safety benefit and instead increases the Harmful Score (HS).

D.8 Router Evaluation

To evaluate the classification performance and generalization ability of the router, we fine-tune Llama3.1 on SST2 and evaluate the router on unseen data constructed from DirectHarm4 and AGNEWS. We report the AUROC, TPR, FPR, and benign over refusal rate under different routing thresholds τ\tau.

As shown in Table 20, the router achieves an AUROC of 100%, indicating strong separation between harmful and benign inputs. When τ=0\tau=0, the router achieves a TPR of 100%, an FPR of 0%, and a benign over refusal rate of 0%. Increasing τ\tau beyond 0 gradually reduces the TPR, while decreasing τ\tau increases both the FPR and benign over refusal rate. These results support τ=0\tau=0 as the default threshold and demonstrate that the router generalizes well to unseen data distributions.

Appendix E Related Work

E.1 Alignment-stage and Fine-tuning-stage Defenses

Existing defenses can be classified by the stage at which they intervene. Alignment-stage methods harden the model before user adaptation, for example through perturbation-aware alignment, data and representation hardening, tamper-resistant alignment, defensive response guidance, or post-alignment safety enhancement.

Perturbation-aware alignment. Vaccine [15] enhances large models’ resistance to harmful fine-tuning through a perturbation-aware alignment strategy. The related Booster method [14] augments the alignment objective with a regularization term that attenuates harmful perturbations, thereby strengthening the model’s robustness against subsequent harmful fine-tuning. VAA [3] identifies alignment examples that are particularly vulnerable to forgetting, partitions them into vulnerable and invulnerable groups, and employs group distributionally robust optimization with group-dependent adversarial perturbations to encourage balanced robustness across alignment data.

Data and representation hardening. Ctrl [28] curates clean training data according to model perplexity and uses the selected data to improve robustness against training-based jailbreak attacks. RepNoise [37] reduces the information content of harmful internal representations within the model, making it more difficult for subsequent harmful fine-tuning to recover harmful behaviors while preserving general capabilities and trainability on benign tasks.

Tamper-resistant alignment and defensive response guidance. TAR [40] establishes tamper-resistant safety protections for open-source large language models, enabling them to maintain safety constraints even after extensive fine-tuning. Its robustness is evaluated in settings involving restricted weaponization knowledge and refusal of harmful requests, demonstrating substantially improved resistance to subsequent fine-tuning. SDD [5] steers the model to generate high-quality but irrelevant responses to malicious instructions, causing malicious fine-tuning to incur substantial utility degradation as harmful behavior is learned and thereby increasing resistance to malicious adaptation.

Safety-subspace extrapolation. LoX [34] is a training-free post-alignment defense that strengthens safety-critical low-rank subspaces by extrapolating the low-rank components of safety-alignment weight updates, thereby improving robustness against subsequent benign and malicious fine-tuning while preserving adaptability to downstream tasks.

Fine-tuning-stage methods instead intervene during user adaptation by filtering or scoring training data, regularizing parameter updates, alternating between safety and task objectives, or dynamically shaping safety objectives and augmenting safety data. Earlier studies established the motivation for such defenses. Qi et al. [35] demonstrated that safety alignment can be substantially degraded by fine-tuning with only a few adversarial examples and can even deteriorate unintentionally when models are fine-tuned on benign downstream data. Bianchi et al. [1] showed that incorporating a small proportion of safety demonstrations into instruction fine-tuning can substantially improve model safety while largely preserving general capabilities.

Filtering or scoring data. BDS [10] formulates defense against harmful fine-tuning from a Bayesian inference perspective and adaptively schedules training examples according to their estimated safety risks, enabling an attack-agnostic defense across diverse attack scenarios.

Regularizing updates. [19] propose an EMA-based optimization strategy that stabilizes fine-tuning dynamics and substantially reduces harmful response rates without requiring additional safety data. SaLoRA [22] introduces a fixed safety module derived from safety data together with task-specific initialization, constraining low-rank adaptation so that task learning interferes less with safety-related feature directions. AsFT [48] applies alignment-direction regularization to suppress safety-degrading gradient updates, thereby preserving both safety and downstream-task performance. LDIFS [32] regularizes fine-tuning by penalizing the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance between feature representations of the original and fine-tuned models, thereby reducing concept forgetting while preserving downstream-task performance; although not originally designed specifically for harmful fine-tuning, its feature-preservation principle provides a relevant regularization strategy for mitigating the loss of pretrained behaviors during adaptation. SAP [43] introduces safety-aware perturbations during gradient propagation to identify and suppress safety-degrading update directions, mitigating safety degradation while preserving downstream-task performance. More generally, latent adversarial training [2] injects adversarial perturbations into hidden representations during training to improve robustness against unforeseen failure modes such as backdoors and held-out attacks. Although not designed specifically for harmful fine-tuning, it represents a related training-time strategy for improving robustness to adversarial model adaptation.

Alternating between safety and task objectives. Lisa [12] alternates optimization between an alignment dataset and user data while incorporating a proximal term to limit parameter drift, thereby mitigating the degradation of safety alignment during fine-tuning.

Safety shaping and augmentation. STAR-DSS [33] proposes a dynamic safety shaping framework that assigns fine-grained safety scores to the generated response and uses these signals to dynamically shape the training objective, suppressing unsafe behavior while preserving model utility. SafeStyle [45] shows that augmenting fine-tuning with a small set of safety examples whose styles match the downstream training distribution can substantially preserve safety after fine-tuning.

While effective, fine-tuning-stage defenses generally require modifying the user-adaptation pipeline and may additionally rely on auxiliary safety data, safety scorers or guardrail models, or assumptions about the fine-tuning distribution.

E.2 Post-fine-tuning-stage Defenses

Existing post-fine-tuning-stage defense methods repair safety after user adaptation has already taken place and can be broadly categorized into four paradigms: subspace or localized parameter recovery, parameter rollback, perturbation, or pruning, data-efficient realignment, and inference-time intervention.

Subspace and localized parameter recovery. Safe LoRA [8] projects LoRA weight updates onto a safety-aligned subspace, substantially reducing safety risks without requiring additional retraining. Similarly, LSSF [55] employs low-rank safety subspace fusion, using layer-wise singular-value information to determine safety-critical ranks and recover safety-related low-rank components while preserving downstream utility. NLSR [50] performs neuron-level safety recovery by identifying safety-critical neurons and selectively transplanting safety-related parameter patches from a safety reference model into the compromised model, avoiding full-model retraining while limiting downstream utility degradation.

Rollback, Perturbation, and Pruning. [47] propose a gradient-guided selective weight recovery and rollback mechanism that identifies and restores safety-relevant parameters while limiting degradation of downstream-task performance. Panacea [41] restores safety alignment by injecting adaptively optimized perturbations into the model after fine-tuning, optimizing the perturbation to improve safety while preserving downstream utility. Antidote [11] identifies and prunes parameters associated with harmful behavior after fine-tuning to counter harmful fine-tuning attacks, while exhibiting robustness across different hyperparameter settings.

Data-efficient realignment. One-shot FT [52] employs bilevel optimization to select a single safety-patch instance and uses it for efficient post-fine-tuning realignment while preserving task utility.

Inference-Time Intervention. MetaDefense [18] trains the LLM to follow dedicated defense prompts that are invoked both before and during generation, enabling the model to assess the harmfulness of user queries and partially generated responses and terminate potentially harmful outputs proactively during generation.

E.3 Layer-wise Safety Analysis

Recent work demonstrates that safety behavior is not uniformly distributed across model layers. Safety Layers [23] identifies safety-critical layers and further proposes SPPFT, which protects these layers during fine-tuning to mitigate safety degradation. LARF [21] identifies safety-sensitive layers and leverages their representations to detect and filter fine-tuning examples that are likely to degrade safety alignment. These studies establish the importance of layer-wise safety localization, but their localization criteria do not explicitly characterize the direction of a layer’s effect on refusal.

SLDR belongs to the post-fine-tuning setting, yet it differs by localizing recovery to a small set of safety-sensitive layers and applying the recovery adapter conditionally rather than as a fixed model-level intervention. Specifically, SLDR extends prior layer-wise diagnostics by introducing a signed measure that distinguishes, under the scaling probe, layers whose strengthening increases refusal from those whose strengthening decreases refusal, and leverages both ends of this spectrum for selective post-fine-tuning recovery.

Appendix F Limitation

Our method can only use LoRA fine-tuning during the defense stage and does not support full-parameter fine-tuning. During downstream task training, both full-parameter fine-tuning and LoRA fine-tuning can be used. Due to computational resource constraints, we did not conduct experiments on LLMs with larger parameter counts, such as 70B. We only discussed the scenario where an attacker poisons the model by injecting harmful samples, as well as two jailbreak attack scenarios. More complex out-of-distribution (OOD) attacks were not explored. We did not discuss the robustness of representation-based dynamic routing inference. For instance, an attacker could craft adversarial examples such that the malicious score of those examples falls below the threshold, thereby bypassing the dynamic routing inference mechanism.

Appendix G Impact Statement

This paper proposed SLDR, a defense framework against malicious fine-tuning attacks on LLMs. The positive societal impact of this work lies in enhancing the safety and trustworthiness of LLMs deployed in fine-tuning-as-a-service scenarios. The analysis of experimental results in this paper may introduce potential for malicious exploitation. However, we believe that the defensive benefits of this work significantly outweigh such risks. Disclaimer: This paper contains model-generated content that may be offensive.
